title: Is your employer spying on you?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck examine whether employers spy on employees. They cover the legal landscape (employers can monitor company networks and devices, and courts mostly side with employers), common surveillance methods (packet sniffers in promiscuous mode, desktop monitoring/keylogging software, log files, phone and email interception, GPS and keycard tracking, CCTV cameras), the Pillsbury case where an employee was fired over emails and lost in court, the IKEA France private investigator scandal, and how employees might detect monitoring software by checking running processes. They also discuss states requiring notice (Connecticut and Delaware), bans on demanding social media passwords, and bring-your-own-device trends. The episode ends with a listener mail from Norbert in Hungary about greetings on support calls, a digression about Budapest's hospital museum, and sign-off details.
topics: how to detect spyware on work computer
employee fired for social media posts

segments.title: Opening banter and premise
segments.summary: Hosts joke about paranoia and introduce the question of whether employers spy on workers, noting employees often implicitly consent through contracts and that Connecticut and Delaware require notice.

segments.title: Prevalence and statistics on employer monitoring
segments.summary: Hosts cite dated survey figures on firings for email misuse and internet misuse, and note that employers can monitor but generally focus on flagged employees. They discuss employees being fired for talking about the company or harassment.

segments.title: Pillsbury case and legal stance
segments.summary: The Pillsbury employee was fired over emails that criticized coworkers and mocked the company Christmas party; he sued but lost, as the court said company devices and networks can be monitored. Employers can legally lie about surveillance.
topics: employer legal rights on company networks

segments.title: Ways employers spy: overview
segments.summary: The hosts list the main methods: packet sniffers, log files, desktop monitoring programs, phones, and CCTV cameras, with GPS and keycard tracking as additional methods.

segments.title: Packet sniffers
segments.summary: Packet sniffers normally handle network diagnostics but can be set to promiscuous mode to capture all traffic, including websites visited and emails sent, when placed on a computer or company server.

segments.title: Desktop monitoring and log files
segments.summary: Desktop monitoring software can log keystrokes and intercept video output, often installed remotely by administrators. Deleted files and log files can still reveal activity and be used against employees.

segments.title: Phone eavesdropping and email interception law
segments.summary: Employers may eavesdrop on work phone calls, using a loophole allowing monitoring of job-related talk after a brief check. Under the ECPA, phone calls in transit are protected but stored emails on servers are not, so emails can be copied legally.

segments.title: Bring your own device and personal accounts
segments.summary: Hosts discuss bring-your-own-device policies and how company networks allow monitoring even of personal accounts, while HTTPS does not protect activity on work networks.

segments.title: Detecting monitoring software
segments.summary: Forbes advice on checking Task Manager or Activity Monitor for unfamiliar processes and comparing with a coworker's computer. Companies keep whitelists of approved monitoring software.

segments.title: Social media, cameras, and the IKEA France case
segments.summary: States have outlawed demands for social media passwords. Employees can be fired for personal blog posts. Office cameras may capture screens. IKEA France hired a private investigator to check on an employee on sick leave, using improperly obtained personal data.

segments.title: Listener mail: Norbert from Hungary
segments.summary: Norbert, an I.T. support worker in Hungary, asks why American callers don't greet him. The hosts offer theories about stress over malfunctioning computers and apologize on behalf of Americans. They then discuss Budapest's underground hospital museum.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: Hosts recap, point listeners to tech stuff and a site search, and give social media and email contact details.
